name: Calgary Barbell programmes

card.summary: Structured strength programmes from the Calgary Barbell coaching brand, followed by lifters who build muscle and strength for a stronger-looking physique and peak for competition.
card.note: Heavy peaking-style training carries injury risk; one forum user reported a knee injury while running such programming.

quick.overview:
Calgary Barbell is a strength-training business whose programming and videos are followed by powerlifters and gym-goers. Its programmes are structured, multi-week plans built around the squat, bench press and deadlift, and are discussed as peaking-style or advanced plans. For looks, the relevance is the usual one for heavy barbell training: more strength work over time builds muscle, which supports a more muscular, athletic physique.

The brand's site lists an app, coaching, nutrition and a free 16-week programme. Lifters on forums mention running its programming alongside other methods such as Sheiko, and cite its form-check videos and grip tips.
quick.how: Followers pick a programme, often the free 16-week plan or one delivered through coaching or the app, and run it over its set weeks, sometimes finishing with a deload. Forum users describe combining the plan with warm-ups focused on core and glutes, and using its coach's form feedback.
quick.risks: Heavy low-rep training and peaking plans load joints and tendons substantially. A T Nation user wrote that after doing Calgary Barbell programming and a 200 kg squat he injured his left knee. Individual response varies, and coaches normally suggest qualified supervision.

lead: Calgary Barbell, whose tagline reads 'Resilience Through Resistance', is a strength-training business that offers an app, coaching, nutrition services, apparel, a gym membership and a free 16-week programme.[1] Its training plans, often called 'Calgary Barbell programmes' or 'CBB programmes', are structured, week-by-week strength plans that lifters use to progress on the squat, bench press and deadlift.

In looksmaxxing circles, strength programmes serve the body side of improvement: consistent progressive resistance training is a standard route to adding muscle, and a broader, more muscular frame is a goal in physique-focused communities. The Calgary Barbell plans are mainly discussed among powerlifting-oriented lifters on forums such as T Nation, where members mention running the 16-week programme, comparing it with Sheiko-style programming, and learning technique from its coach Bryce Krawczyk's form-check videos.[2][3][4]

chain: Follow a structured multi-week barbell plan
Progressive overload on the main lifts and planned peaking
More strength and muscle mass over time
angle.text: The programmes give lifters a planned schedule for heavy compound lifts, which supports the strength and muscle gains that make up a stronger-looking physique.

paras: The company's website lists a CBB app, coaching, nutrition, apparel, gym membership and a free programme whose address points to a 16-week plan.[1] Forum posts describe lifters 'running the Calgary Barbell 16 week program', then considering other programming such as the Sheiko Gold app.[3]

Programmes of this kind belong to the tradition of periodisation, a cyclical way to plan training in phases with the aim of peaking for key competitions, with a taper before the main event. It was formalised by Matveyev around 1964, is widely used in resistance training, and has been questioned by some reviewers who argue evidence for strict sequential blocks is weak.[5]

Posters on T Nation mention the brand in several ways: one planned to have his programming done by a Calgary Barbell coach, another points others to its form-check videos, where the coach advises the knees stay in place at the start of the ascent, and others recommend a 'last rep hook' grip approach used for higher-rep deadlift sets, switching from straps to hook grip on the final rep.[2][6][7] A user who ran Calgary Barbell programming between other plans reported a knee injury after a heavy squat.[8]
No studies found on Calgary Barbell programmes specifically. Research on periodised resistance training generally is summarised in reviews, including critical ones.[5]
